Thursday through Friday morning: A low pressure system moving 
eastward over central Canada will result in a cold front passage 
Thursday afternoon and evening. Main impacts will be gusty winds, 
which will result in fire weather concerns in areas with dry fuels 
and localized blowing dust. This dry cold frontal passage will 
result in little rain, with mountain areas in the ID Panhandle 
expected to receive a trace. 

Ahead of the cold frontal passage, winds will pick up out of the 
west on Thursday morning due to a tightening east-west pressure 
gradient. Areas that will see the strongest winds are the Cascade 
gaps, Wenatchee, Waterville Plateau, and Columbia Basin areas. 
These areas have a good chance (50 percent and above) at seeing 
wind gusts reach 30 mph. Elsewhere, such as in the Moses Lake, 
Spokane, Palouse, and Lewiston/Pullman area will see wind gusts 
20 to 25 mph. Impacts from these winds include blowing objects 
and trouble driving, particularly for high profile vehicles. 

These winds will result in chances for additional hazards throughout 
the Columbia Basin and Waterville Plateau: elevated fire weather 
concerns and potential blowing dust. Dry conditions preceding the 
frontal passage will result in minimum relative humidity values of 
20 to 25 percent throughout much of the Columbia Basin, Waterville, 
Palouse, and Spokane areas. These areas have also seen very little 
measurable rainfall as of late, which has resulted in dry fuels. All 
of these factors will come together tomorrow and create elevated 
fire weather conditions across these areas. Main impacts will be to 
any existing fires, which could see rapid fire spread. Additionally, 
and in a more localized area, dry soils combined with these winds 
create a blowing dust concern, particularly from moses Lake to 
Ritzville. Blowing dust can bring visibilities down to a mile or 
lower, impacting drivers. 

Due to very dry mid and upper levels, this cold front will end up 
producing little rainfall. Portions of the Idaho Panhandle will see 
some rain, but have little chance (less than 15 percent) of seeing 
0.10 inches of rain or more. Despite the dry nature of the front, 
moisture from increased PoPs will result in a chance of fog over 
sheltered northern valleys in the Panhandle. 

Friday evening through Sunday: In the wake of the cold front, zonal 
flow will briefly prevail over the area on Friday as a stronger low 
pressure system develops off the coast of British Columbia. 
Temperatures on Friday will be nearly 10 degrees colder than on 
Thursday. With highs on Friday expected in the high 60s to low 70s, 
these temperatures are lower than normal for this time of year. 

On Friday night, the low will move southward and over the PNW coast. 
Ahead of the main low passage on Saturday morning, winds will again 
increase throughout much of the area, though this time winds will 
increase from the north as a north-south surface pressure gradient 
strengthens. Wind gusts through the Basin, Waterville Plateau, and 
Okanogan Valley could reach 30-35 mph Saturday morning and 
afternoon. As the low tracks eastward, winds begin to increase in 
the Idaho Panhandle on Saturday night and continue to be elevated 
with gusts 20-25 mph through Sunday morning. Ridgetops could see 
wind gusts up to 35 mph. Impacts with these wind gusts include 
blowing objects and trouble driving, especially for high profile 
vehicles. 

Saturday night into Sunday, models show the center of the low moving 
across the Washington/Oregon border, resulting in PoPs over the 
entire forecast area increasing to nearly 70 percent. Expected 
rainfall show much of the forecast area receiving a quarter inch of 
rain or more. Lowest chances (20 to 30 percent) are seen further 
north, such as near Omak and Colville, as well as in the Moses Lake 
area. This is where the main uncertainty with this system comes in. 
Models are struggling with the track the low takes, and how quickly 
the low will move past the area. This has introduced significant 
spread in expected precipitation totals. Differences between the 
25th and 75th percentiles are nearly an inch in SE Washington and 
central Idaho, which are the areas that will see the highest rain 
totals.

Alongside this rainfall, chances for isolated thunderstorms increase 
as the low moves through. Areas from Spokane to Wenatchee and 
southward have a 10 to 20 percent chance of thunderstorms. Mid to 
long range models show CAPE values increasing a couple hundred J/kg, 
and steep 3-6km lapse rates. The track of the low being uncertain 
also makes thunderstorm coverage over the area uncertain.
Even now, many models show the highest chances for thunderstorms 
outside of our forecast area to the south and east. However, with 
PWATs 0.5 inches and above, it is worth mentioning since these 
thunderstorms could yield isolated heavy rainfall rates that could 
lead to debris flows or flooding.
